newsitem.title: UK: British utility shares factor in Labour's tax take.
newsitem.headline: British utility shares factor in Labour's tax take.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party said on Wednesday that utility stocks have already priced in its proposed windfall profits levy, but analysts said questions remain over how much and how wide the net will be cast.
"I believe the levy is discounted in the share price already," finance spokesman Gordon Brown told BBC television on Wednesday.
But Labour, well ahead of the ruling Conservative party in polls running up to a May 1 election, has consistently declined to specify income targets for the tax.
The party has also refused to pinpoint companies other than referring to privatised firms which have made "excess profits", and are regulated by statute.

Labour would use the one-off tax to pay for a programme aimed at cutting unemployment which has been estimated to cost three billion pounds ($5 billion), but Brown is thought by many analysts to be targeting a total revenue of around five billion pounds.
"The sector would react badly if the levy is significantly above five billion pounds," said Nigel Hawkins, analyst at Yamaichi.
In a report earlier this month, Goldman Sachs looked at estimates for the impact of such a levy on different companies using a measure of total returns to shareholders against a stock market average.

It concluded that a five billion pound total levy could mean a tax of 2.1-3.5 billion on the electricity sector, 0.8-1.3 billion on water, up to 0.5 billion on gas, between 0.2-0.6 billion for transport and up to 0.4 billion for British Telecommunications (BT).
"These seem broadly to be discounted in current share prices," the report said.
Nikko Europe echoes this view, saying that it believes "the political risk, a windfall tax imposed by a Labour government, has little impact on the current valuation."

Analysts generally feel that water and electricity companies will face a large part of the tax but that the net could also be cast wider, to include BT, the former British Gas utility Centrica and even Railtrack and British Airports Authority.

"They could make the catchment base very broad to minimise legal problems but then set the actual parameters to weigh it towards water and electricity," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.

Labour, which has said it should not face any legal problems over the tax, is expected to put water and electricity stocks high on its target list because of large dividend payouts in the sectors and hefty pay packets since privatisation.
The party has been fiercely critical of payouts from water companies when it claims over 800 million gallons a day are leaking out of pipes.
The electricity sector, which shrunk due to takeovers, leaving just one independent regional firm, Southern, poses the additional problem of levying a retrospective tax on new owners.

The Institute of Fiscal Studies (IFS) said in a report earlier this month that "perhaps the most serious criticism of the windfall levy is that it is unlikely to tax all the owners of the firms who have actually received excess profits from the privatisation."

One of the new owners, CalEnergy, the U.S. independent power group that bought Northern Electric late last year, has already said in its annual report that it had "established a liability" for the tax, thought to be around 100 million pounds.
But perhaps the clearest guide to the implied impact of the tax comes from expectations of share performances if the Conservatives manage to retain power on May 1.
"If the Conservatives win, three to five billion pounds of value will be unlocked straight away," the analyst said.
That is as much as 10 percent of the water and electricity sector's total value on some current estimates.
($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
